title: Playing jazz rather than 'Dixieland' at Nick's
summary: Hackett disliked the word Dixieland; the band played traditional tunes in its own way for the crowd that came to hear them.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: His name was Andy Russo. He had been with the bigger bands, but he had that style. Now this is a new aspect in my life, a sort of a Dixieland -- and I don't like to use that -- Bobby Hackett wouldn't stand still for the word 'Dixieland'.
Well, that's what Bobby liked and that's what I liked --
That's what I remember about Bobby.
He just called it jazz music. I would

call it Chicago style, New Orleans style -- we played a lot of traditional songs, but not in the traditional ways. We didn't copy from the records. That's really what you call traditional playing, you know?
But we played the songs that the people wanted to hear. They could call it Dixieland or whatever. Bobby said we just played jazz music, and that's what we played - and of necessity.
Yes, they come in to hear that.
